That is: those companions, the evil companions, "that they may bar them from the way" [az-Zukhruf: 37], meaning: they divert them and prevent them from the truth and from the straight path, "and they think that they are guided" [az-Zukhruf: 37].

Therefore He said in another place: ﴿And on the day when the wrongdoer will bite his hands, saying, "Oh, would that I had taken a way with the Messenger! Oh, woe to me! Would that I had not taken so-and-so as a friend. He had led me away from the Reminder after it had come to me. And ever is Satan, to man, a deserter."﴾ [al-Furqan: 27-29].

And the evil companions are companions only in this world. As for the Hereafter, they will be enemies, each one blaming his companion: ﴿Close friends that Day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 67].

Likewise, Satan will disown his followers and forsake them in the Hereafter: ﴿And I had over you no authority except that I invited you, and you responded to me. So do not blame me; but blame yourselves﴾ [Ibrahim: 22].

And our Lord, glorified and exalted is He, has taught us how to protect ourselves from Satan, saying: ﴿And if an evil suggestion from Satan should tempt you, then seek refuge in Allah﴾ [al-A'raf: 200].

Concerning His words, Exalted is He: ﴿the distance of the two easts﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 38]. It is the distance between the east and the west. This manner of speech is called in the language (al-taghlib, "predominance by one of two opposites"), because the east has the west opposite it, and the Arabs, in paired opposites, give precedence to one over the other, just as they say, for example, of the two shaykhs Abu Bakr and Umar, "al-Umarayn" (the two Umars).

And when we reflect on the east and the west from the astronomical and geographical standpoint, we find that the east is the west of others, and the west is the east of others. Thus, both are east, and both are west.

Because this is a common affliction that includes everyone. When affliction strikes one man among people, it is hard for him to bear, and it weighs on him that he should grieve while others are happy. But when the affliction becomes general, it becomes easier and its burden is lightened for the group, because of the feeling of sharing it, even if the sharing is in grief.

This meaning was expressed by al-Khansa' in her elegy for her brother Sakhr, when she said:

Were it not for the abundance of those weeping around me
over their brothers, I would have killed myself.

And they do not weep like my brother, but I console myself for him with consolation.

And another poet said:

What softened the blows of calamities is that I,
even if they crushed me, am not alone in their bitterness.

Yes, when calamities become general they become easier to bear, but this applies to the calamities of this world. As for the calamity of the Hereafter, it is not made easier and not lightened: ﴿And it will not benefit you today﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 39], that is, the Day of Resurrection, ﴿since you have wronged yourselves, that in the punishment you will be sharing﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 39].

The meaning: (The address here is to our master, the Messenger of God (ﷺ).) Spare yourself, O Muhammad, do not exhaust yourself or burden yourself with what you cannot bear in the cause of guiding these people.

He described them as deaf and blind, although in reality they see and hear. They hear the truth but do not follow it, and they see the straight path but do not walk it. So they become like the deaf man who does not hear, and like the blind man who does not see.

For this reason He, glory be to Him, said elsewhere: ﴿For indeed, it is not the eyes that are blinded, but blinded are the hearts which are within the breasts﴾ [al-Hajj: 46]. So they are averse, obstinate, and arrogant in accepting the truth.

This is the meaning of error in ﴿And whoever is in manifest error﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 40].

And is there any error more evident and clearer than the error of one who sees the truth and does not follow it?

The Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, does not address His Prophet (ﷺ) with this address unless he was truly distressing himself and nearly destroying himself in the cause of his call. Therefore his Lord addressed him saying: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over them, if they do not believe in this message﴾ [al-Kahf: 6], and His address with the words ﴿Upon you is only the conveying﴾ [ash-Shura: 48]. That is because the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was loving of his message, loving of his methodology, and loving of his entire community. He wished to make them taste what he had tasted of the sweetness of faith, and he wished to practise in himself that you love for your brother what you love for yourself.

O Muhammad, be at ease. If you die, We will show you their punishment and Our retribution against them in the Hereafter. If you remain alive, We will show you their punishment hastened for them in this world.

The meaning of ﴿that which We promised them﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 42] is: the punishment of this world before the punishment of the Hereafter. ﴿Indeed We are Omnipotent over them﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 42]. "Muqtadirun" (Omnipotent) is an intensive form (mubalagha) of "qadir" (capable). The meaning is: We have power over them and are able to bring punishment upon them, and they will not escape from Us.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 43, verse 44:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And indeed, it﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 44], i.e., the noble Qur'an with which you were sent, O Muhammad. This Book is a methodology for life, and it is an everlasting miracle that remains until the Hour is established. ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 44], meaning: a source of honour, might and pride for you and for your people, i.e., the Arabs, because it was revealed in Arabic. How many peoples have gained might through the might of their languages.

So it is an honour for the Arabic language, and an honour for every Arab that the Qur'an was revealed in it. A human being by his nature loves pride, loves fame and the spreading of renown, and it is not hidden from anyone today that it is the Qur'an that has given the Arabic language its standing among the languages of the world.

Had it not been for the Qur'an, Arabic would have vanished just as other languages have vanished, and we now find many people of other nations turning eagerly to learning Arabic and mastering it, so that they may be able to memorise the Qur'an, interpret it, and understand its meanings.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 43, verse 45:

Here is a pause for reflection, so that we may understand the verse: ﴿And ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers﴾. How can the Messenger of Allah ask them when they are dead? Why does his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, command him with this command? When Allah, glorified is He, commands His Messenger with a command, it becomes obligatory upon him to obey.

Allah, glorified is He, prepared this opportunity for His Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, during the journey of the Isra' and Mi'raj (Night Journey and Ascension), where he indeed met his brother prophets who came before him, gathered with them, and led them in prayer as imam in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), while they were dead according to the law of death, and he was alive according to the law of the living.

It is established that he addressed some of them and spoke with them, just as he spoke with our master Musa, peace be upon him, and that he went back and forth with him regarding the matter of the fifty prayers, until Allah made them five.

If you say: how can the two opposites, dead and alive, come together, and there be speech and mutual understanding between them? We say: this is possible, because it is an act of power, and the absoluteness of power belongs to Allah, exalted is He. The absoluteness of power is not bound by the laws of the living and the dead.

We have said before that we should attribute the act to its doer so that we may be at rest. This matter is of the unseen (ghayb) which we believe in, and we attribute every wonder in it to the one who originated this wonder.

You remember the story of our master Ibrahim when they threw him into the fire. What happened? The law is that fire burns. But what if Allah willed it to be coolness and safety while it was still a blazing fire? When Allah willed it, it was coolness and safety upon Ibrahim, and the law of burning was suspended in it.

Had He, glorified is He, willed, He could have subjected to this fire a cloud to rain upon it until it was extinguished. Had He willed, they would not have been able to reach Ibrahim nor seize him. But so that the miracle might be completed, Allah enabled them over Ibrahim, and they indeed cast him into the fire while it was blazing, and yet it did not burn him. This is the absoluteness of power.

Likewise we see the absoluteness of power in the story of the staff of our master Musa, when he struck the sea with it and it split, and the water congealed in it until each part became like a great mountain. And it is the same staff with which he struck the rock and twelve springs gushed forth from it. So Allah gives us snapshots of the absoluteness of power and the breaking of custom and laws, so that we may measure by them.

Some exegetes find this matter far-fetched. That is, the meeting between the living and the dead, and they interpret the meaning in a way that agrees with their inclinations, saying: the intended meaning is "ask the followers of the messengers before you, because they took the religion from them." The adherents of this opinion want to escape the question of the living meeting the dead, and from affirming this miracle that breaks custom. But there is no strangeness in that and no wonder, because the doer is who? Allah.

Or: the intended meaning of ﴿And ask those whom We sent before you﴾ is not the asking itself nor the answer itself; rather the intended meaning is admonition and taking lesson, in the manner of the words of the preacher, for example, in the Friday sermon: "Ask the earth, who made rivers flow in it, and who made trees grow in it; ask the meadow adorned; ask the water flowing..." etc. So the meaning is not that we should ask the earth; rather we ask ourselves, reflect and contemplate.

Likewise in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers﴾.

But the Messenger of Allah did not ask those before him of the messengers about this matter: ﴿Did We appoint, besides the Most Merciful, gods to be worshipped?﴾ The reality is that he did not ask. Why? Because he has such certainty that makes him independent of this question. The Messenger of Allah has no need of one who confirms to him that there are no gods worshipped alongside Allah.

Therefore it is reported from Imam Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that he said: "If the veil were lifted from me, I would not increase in certainty." Meaning: I believe in the unseen with a firm and settled faith, as if I looked upon it and saw it, and if it were revealed to me nothing would increase my certainty, because Allah's report to His messenger about a thing is more truthful than our seeing it...

The interrogative in ﴿Did We appoint, besides the Most Merciful, gods to be worshipped?﴾ is intended for negation and denunciation. Worship of other than Allah is a matter that did not come from the messengers. Therefore it is the making of humans, which they invented to satisfy their desires, to have for themselves an object of worship, but an object of worship according to their whims, an object of worship that does not restrict their appetites and desires with a method of "do this" and "do not do this."

From here they worshipped idols, and worshipped the sun, the moon, the stars and others, all of which are objects of worship by their own claim, ﴿for which Allah sent down no authority﴾, and which He did not legislate in any of the revealed laws.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 43, verse 46:

We said: The "āyāt" (signs, here meaning miracles) are the miracles that demonstrate the truthfulness of the Messenger in conveying from God. Our master Mūsā (peace be upon him) was among the most abundantly endowed of the messengers with miracles and extraordinary signs, and this means that his people were among the most obstinate of God's creation and the most averse to the methodology. God the Exalted says: ﴿And We indeed gave Mūsā nine clear signs﴾ [al-Isrā': 101].

What is the relevance of the Qur'an bringing an episode from the story of our master Mūsā at this point? They said: Because the disbelievers of Makkah had gathered and stood against the call, and they objected to the call coming through Muḥammad specifically. So they said: ﴿And they said, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of importance from the two cities?"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31].

They mean Makkah, where there was al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, and al-Ṭā'if, where there was ʿUrwah ibn Masʿūd al-Thaqafī, and others of the chiefs of the people, the possessors of wealth, rank and prestige among their people.

Thus: the objection was not to the Qur'an itself, but to the one through whose hands the Qur'an came.

Therefore God, glorified is He, willed to give them an example from the procession of the messages: this Mūsā, peace be upon him, was neither a man of wealth, nor a man of rank or authority, and God sent him to one who was more severe in disbelief than the people of Makkah and their chieftains: He sent him to Pharaoh, who not only opposed the call to God but used to say: "I am a god."

Thus: there is no wonder in the sending of Muḥammad, who was from the common people and their poor, to the wealthy lords, namely al-Walīd, ʿUrwah and others of the heads of disbelief, who were more severe than Pharaoh.

Thus the message does not require that the Messenger be a man of wealth, nor a man of rank or authority. Then, this is the mercy of God, which He distributes as He wills, chooses for it whom He wills, and selects from among His servants.

And one who reflects on the missions of Mūsā and Muḥammad finds that Mūsā's life among his society was less than Muḥammad's life among his society, because Mūsā was raised in Pharaoh's house until he grew up, and the incident of killing occurred in which Mūsā killed a man from the people. Then a man came from the farthest part of the city and said: ﴿O Mūsā, indeed the chiefs are conspiring about you to kill you, so leave; indeed I am to you of the sincere advisers.* So he left from it, fearful, watchful. He said: My Lord, save me from the wrongdoing people﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 20-21].

After that he arrived at Madyan, and there he found: ﴿And when he came to the water of Madyan, he found upon it a group of people watering, and he found beside them two women holding back. He said, "What is your circumstance?" They said, "We cannot water until the shepherds have driven off, and our father is an old man." * So he watered for them; then he turned to the shade and said, "My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need"﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 23-24].

First: we say that these verses give us a methodology and a constitution for dealing with the Muslim woman, and how and when she goes out of her house. The reason for the going out of these two women was that their father was an old man, and there was no one to take care of their needs.

Thus: a woman should not leave her house except out of necessity, and when she goes out she should be modest, veiled, and not mix with men. Then the duty of the faith-based community is to respect the right of the woman and to take her hand in what she wishes to do of work, because it is a community of mercy and kinship among all Muslims.

I recall that the first time we traveled to Makkah, in the year 1950, we were living in the house of a well-off man, who would volunteer and take us to work in his private car. Once, as we were driving, he saw in front of one of the houses a wooden board on which dough is placed, and the door of the house was closed, so he got down, took the board into his car and left.

When I asked him about that, he said: "By God, we have a custom: when we see the door closed and something like this in front of it, we know that the owner of the house is absent and the people of the house need something, so we fulfill it for them." The point is that the man took the dough board, filled it with bread, according to what God had decreed for him, and returned it to its owners.

This is the meaning we have learned from the story of our master Mūsā: ﴿So he watered for them﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 24]. And we return to the story: ﴿then he turned to the shade and said, "My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need"﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 24]. That is: Mūsā was a poor man, possessing nothing of the world except his physical strength. This one who sits under the shade of a tree has no shelter; is there any greater humility and weakness than that?

This indicates that he was a man (ghalbān, i.e. unfortunate) who possessed nothing of the world's goods. If we compare him with Muḥammad, we find that Muḥammad remained longest among his people, for he grew up among them from his birth, and he used to herd the sheep of his family for a wage. When he grew up he engaged in trade, and he was, as we say, the "manager of affairs" of Lady Khadījah, and he would earn and have wealth.

Yet God sent Mūsā, who was weaker than Muḥammad, to Pharaoh, who was stronger and more severe than al-Walīd, ʿUrwah and others. And with this we understand why the mention of our master Mūsā came at this place: ﴿And indeed We sent Mūsā with Our signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 46].

Then there is another point of weakness in the mission of our master Mūsā: that he was sent to Pharaoh, who had been raised in his house. Therefore God, the Exalted, taught him how to approach him in the matter of the call, because Pharaoh used to remind him of favour: ﴿[Pharaoh] said, "Did we not raise you among us as a child, and you remained among us for years of your life?"﴾ [al-Shuʿarā': 18]. So God taught him to speak to him with gentle speech: ﴿So speak to him gently; perhaps he will be reminded or fear﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 44].

And His saying: ﴿with Our signs﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 46], that is: with the manifest miracles that accompanied the call of our master Mūsā, to support him and establish for the people the truthfulness of his conveying from God. We have said that a miracle must be a matter of challenge, such that no one can bring its like, and that it must be of the kind in which the people excelled, so that the challenge has meaning; otherwise, how could I challenge you with something you neither know nor are skilled in?

And because the people of Mūsā excelled in sorcery, the miracle of the staff was among the miracles that God the Exalted gave to our master Mūsā, and his Lord, mighty and majestic, trained him in the use of this staff and made him aware of what secrets it contains before his meeting with Pharaoh.

Read: ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Mūsā? * He said, "It is my staff; I lean upon it, and I beat down [leaves] with it for my sheep, and I have in it other uses." * He said, "Throw it down, O Mūsā." * So he threw it down, and suddenly it was a snake, moving swiftly﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 17-20].

This situation was a training for Mūsā in using his miracle before Pharaoh, and then Mūsā knew that if his uses for his staff were to lean upon it and to beat down [leaves] for his sheep, then God the Exalted has other uses beyond these apparent uses.

Therefore we have seen some orientalists say: the Qur'an repeated the story of Mūsā's staff in more than one place. The reality is that the story contains no repetition; rather, these are different situations of the staff with Mūsā. The first time, as we said, was a training for Mūsā, so that he would not be surprised by what the staff does if he throws it before Pharaoh.

The second time was before Pharaoh, and the third when Pharaoh gathered the magicians.

Thus: there is no repetition in the matter; rather, these are different situations of one thing. And when the Qur'an presented this story to us, it taught us the difference between sorcery and miracle: sorcery is imagination and deception of the sight, whereas the miracle is a real, actual fact.

Therefore He said of the staff: ﴿and suddenly it was a snake, moving swiftly﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 20], that is, in actual reality. And when He spoke of the cords of the magicians, He said: ﴿It appeared to him, because of their magic, that they were moving swiftly﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 66]. The proof of this is that the magicians and the people of skill and experience in this field, when they saw the staff suddenly turn into a snake, fell down prostrating and believed in Mūsā and what he brought, because they were the most knowledgeable of the people in this matter: ﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of Hārūn and Mūsā"﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 70].

And God, the Exalted, says in another place: ﴿They bewitched the eyes of the people and frightened them﴾ [al-A'rāf: 116]. The meaning: they bewitched the eyes of the people, that the matter of sorcery stops at the eye and at sight; it is imagination in the view of the eye only.

Our own life also bears witness to this. I recall that I was head of the al-Azhar mission in Algeria, and there I became acquainted with the Saudi ambassador to Algeria, Shaykh Riyāḍ al-Khaṭīb, son of Fu'ād al-Khaṭīb, the great poet, and a friendship developed between me and him. It happened that he was transferred from Algeria to Pakistan, and after that I travelled to Pakistan and stayed with Shaykh Riyāḍ.

One day we spoke about sorcery, and he said: "I will show you a strange matter: here is an Indian magician who does such and such." I said: "By God, a chance to see what he does." In the morning we went to a village and brought the Indian magician. He sat down and set up a "nuṣba" (a small arrangement), and brought cotton, which he shaped into the form of a rope and twisted it thus. There was a small boy with him, and he gestured to him to climb this rope, until all those sitting saw the boy in fact climbing up the rope.

The next day, after I had reviewed the verses on sorcery in the Book of God, I took with me a photographic camera, and I wished to photograph this scene. Indeed I photographed it, and the next day, after developing it, I found the picture white, with nothing in it at all.

My companion said to me: "Then how do you explain this imagination which we saw?" I said: "By God, from the Qur'anic account concerning the jinn we know that they take all forms, and there is no objection at all that the magician seeks the help of the jinn. God the Exalted says: ﴿And that there were men among mankind who sought refuge with men among the jinn, so they increased them in burden﴾ [al-Jinn: 6]."

Thus: there is no rational objection that the magician should subject from among the jinn one who helps him in this matter, and who takes whatever form he wishes.

The noble Qur'an has stated that the signs and miracles with which our master Mūsā was sent were nine signs: ﴿And We indeed gave Mūsā nine clear signs. So ask the Children of Israel, when he came to them, and Pharaoh said to him, "Indeed, I think you, O Mūsā, are bewitched"﴾ [al-Isrā': 101].

And He said in another place: ﴿And We did not show them a sign except that it was greater than its sister...﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 48], and this means that they were many signs, clear, manifest and evident.

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 46]. The malaʾ (chiefs) are the people, especially the notables among them, and those of standing, from our saying: "So-and-so is ملءَ العين (a fill of the eye)," i.e. imposing in appearance. In another verse He said: ﴿And Qārūn, Pharaoh and Hāmān; and Mūsā had certainly come to them with clear proofs, but they were arrogant in the land, and they were not those who could escape﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 39].

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So he said, "Indeed I am a messenger of the Lord of the worlds"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 46] is a summary of his mission and a concise statement of what he brought.

In the previous verse of Surat al-Ankabut, their reaction was shown to be arrogance (istikbar), and istikbar here means that they knew Musa was upon the truth and that he possessed miracles, yet they were arrogant about believing in him. Here the verse shows another aspect of istikbar.

﴿Then, behold, they laughed at them.﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 47] "They laughed" either out of admiration for the miracle and for the sign they saw, that it was extraordinary and contrary to everything they had seen from the magicians, or they laughed in mockery and derision.

**Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 43, verse 48:**

"Ayah" (sign) means a miracle. ﴿Each one is greater than its sister﴾ means that every miracle is greater and clearer than the one before it. This shows that the inimitability (i'jaz) is evident in all the signs, despite their number. Each sign is great in some respect, because the purpose of the signs is to demonstrate inimitability and to establish something beyond the power and capacity of human beings. As long as each sign fulfils this purpose, it is a great sign.

As for His words, ﴿And We seized them with punishment﴾, that is, We punished them for their denial with a punishment. The Real, glory be to Him, clarified this punishment in another place, when He said: ﴿And We certainly seized the people of Pharaoh with years of drought and shortage of fruits, that perhaps they would remember﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:130).

Reflect on the closing phrase of these two verses. In one place it is ﴿that perhaps they would return﴾, and in another ﴿that perhaps they would remember﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:130). God, glory be to Him, does not punish His creatures because He desires to punish them. He punishes them so that they may return to Him. Thus even the punishment here is a mercy towards them.

As for His words, ﴿that perhaps they would return﴾, that is, to return from obstinacy, dispute and stubbornness. But did they return? Never. They remained in their disbelief and denial, even after God seized them with years of drought, meaning famine, the barrenness and dryness of the land, which resulted in the shortage of fruits and the constriction of livelihood.

Then, after all of that, ﴿We sent upon them the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs and the blood, as distinct signs﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:133), meaning clear signs, evident and manifest. They became constricted and emaciated, preoccupied with earning their daily bread. So, having despaired, they went to Musa, peace be upon him, and said: ﴿And they said, "O ...﴾

The word "magician" (sahir) here does not only mean their acknowledgement of his superiority in the field of magic. It means a man skilled at everything, superior to them in magic, in knowledge, and in grasping the affairs of life; there is no one like him.

This reminds us of a situation from the biography of our master the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when

The point here is that sihr (magic) comes to mean general superiority in any aspect of life. So: when they saw Musa's actions, they submitted to him and conceded his superiority over them, even though they did not believe in him. But because they were convinced of his superiority, and indeed of the truthfulness of his call, they went to him and asked him to supplicate for them and to relieve them of the distress of their hardship.

So they said: ﴿O magician, call upon your Lord for us﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 49]. So: they acknowledge his connection to his Lord, but his Lord is also their Lord, as evidenced by ﴿call upon your Lord for us﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 49], and they did not say, for example, "our Lord."

﴿by what He has covenanted with you﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 49], because your Lord obeys you and does for you what you wish, and He promised you the removal of the punishment from those who believe in you. ﴿Indeed, we will be guided﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 49], meaning: if you remove from us what we are in, we will be guided and believe in you.

So then: their saying ﴿Indeed, we are surely guided﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 49] was merely a word spoken with the tongue in hypocrisy, having no backing of truth in reality. For Allah, glorified is He, removed the punishment from them, and they returned to what they had been upon. The meaning of ﴿they break [their word]﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 50] is that they go back to what they had been upon, and break the covenant they had made against themselves that they would be guided.

Here Pharaoh feels the danger, and his standing before his people begins to shake. He feels that Moses is pulling the carpet out from under his feet, as all eyes turn toward him, especially after the incident of the magicians who believed in the Lord of Aaron and Moses and did not wait for Pharaoh's permission.

After the drought had descended upon them, and barrenness had struck them until they despaired, they turned to Moses and asked him to remove what they were suffering. Therefore we see Pharaoh trying to restore his standing and improve his image before his people.

﴿And Pharaoh proclaimed among his people.﴾ What did his herald proclaim?

﴿He said: "O my people, does not the dominion of Egypt belong to me, and these rivers flowing beneath me? Do you not see?"﴾ Meaning: pay attention to my standing, my dominion and my power over you, and do not concern yourselves with the matter of Moses, for I am still the king of Egypt, and the rivers flow beneath me. That is, I am still the benefactor of your blessings.

﴿Do you not see?﴾ But we notice in this proclamation that he said nothing about his divinity. He did not say: "I am your Lord Most High," for he had abandoned these slogans, which no longer had a place after what happened with Moses.

Then consider the form of the address: ﴿Does not the dominion of Egypt belong to me?﴾ with this interrogative of affirmation, meaning: tell me, have I not been a king over you? He did not come with the form of a declarative statement such as: "I am the king of Egypt."

Thus, Pharaoh now speaks from a position of weakness, for he had said previously:

﴿So he said, "I am your Lord Most High."﴾ [An-Nazi'at: 24] and now he says: ﴿Does not the dominion of Egypt belong to me?﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 51]...

His saying: ﴿And Pharaoh proclaimed among his people﴾ — Pharaoh himself did not proclaim; rather he commanded someone to proclaim among the people with this proclamation. Since the proclamation was by his command, it was attributed to him... His saying: ﴿and these rivers flowing beneath me﴾ — the phrase "beneath me" (min tahtī) indicates firm establishment and control, and indeed his palaces were directly on the river, as if the river passed beneath them. And he used the plural "rivers," although we know that in Egypt there is one river, the Nile, which branches into two branches, Damietta and Rosetta, so why did he say ﴿these rivers﴾?

They said: in the days of the Pharaohs there were five rivers, meaning they divided the river into five branches to increase the shorelines, and thus they had ten shorelines upon which their palaces were built.

Pharaoh conducts this comparison between himself and Moses, saying: "I am better than this one," meaning Moses, and he suffices with pointing to him in contempt (mahin), meaning: weak and contemptible, since no power protects him and he has no soldiers to defend him.

﴿And he almost cannot express himself clearly﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 52], i.e., he cannot make himself understood and speak eloquently. The meaning is: he cannot speak with clarity and fluency, because Moses, peace be upon him, had a speech impediment (lathgha) in his tongue.

Therefore it is said that he asked his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, to support him in this matter by sending with him his brother Aaron: ﴿And my brother Aaron, he is more eloquent in tongue than I, so send him with me as a helper, to confirm me. Indeed, I fear that they will deny me﴾ [al-Qasas: 34].

It is narrated that the cause of this impediment in his tongue, when he was young, was that he said a word that showed boldness toward Pharaoh, so that Pharaoh doubted his matter and feared him. They said to Pharaoh: "He is a child who does not know anything." To prove this to Pharaoh, they brought Moses a date and a live coal; he took the coal, and it burned his tongue, and this caused that impediment in him.

This is the same thing as the imagined physical picture that Pharaoh had of the Messenger: that he should come wearing bracelets of gold, which signify power, control and greatness, or that he should come with angels accompanying him, supporting him and bearing witness to his truth.

Al-istikhfaf (making someone frivolous) means haste, levity, and lack of reflection on matters. That is, Pharaoh made them frivolous with this speech, so they obeyed him in the misguidance he was in and agreed with him in corruption. One does not agree with corruption except someone who benefits from it. Or he found them to be people of levity and folly, who did not reflect on matters, so he mocked them with this speech.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 43, verses 55–56:

The meaning of ﴿آسَفُونَا﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 55] is "they angered us," so the result was ﴿ٱنتَقَمْنَا مِنْهُمْ﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 55], "We took vengeance upon them," and how ﴿فَأَغْرَقْنَاهُمْ أَجْمَعِينَ﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 55], "so We drowned them all." By drowning, God made them (salafan), a precedent (al-salaf: those who came before). That is, God made them an example and a lesson for those who come after them, ﴿وَمَثَلاً لِّلآخِرِينَ﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 56], "and an example for those who follow," a lesson for others among the disbelievers.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 43, verses 55–56:

The meaning of ﴿آسَفُونَا﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 55] is "they angered us," so the result was ﴿ٱنتَقَمْنَا مِنْهُمْ﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 55], "We took vengeance upon them," and how ﴿فَأَغْرَقْنَاهُمْ أَجْمَعِينَ﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 55], "so We drowned them all." By drowning, God made them (salafan), a precedent (al-salaf: those who came before). That is, God made them an example and a lesson for those who come after them, ﴿وَمَثَلاً لِّلآخِرِينَ﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 56], "and an example for those who follow," a lesson for others among the disbelievers.

Here the verb ضُرِب (ḍuriba) is in the passive voice, the form for a verb whose doer is not named, so who "struck" the son of Maryam as an example? Allah, glory be to Him, is the One who made the son of Maryam an example, because he was born to a mother without a father and came from the breath of Allah, glory be to Him, into Maryam. They attributed him to God, exalted is Allah far above that by a great exaltation, so Allah refuted them by saying that Jesus is like Adam in creation. ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus with Allah is like the likeness of Adam. He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he is.﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 59] So if Jesus was born without a father, then Adam was born without a father or a mother, and the One who is able to do the greater is able to do the lesser all the more, so do not be led into temptation concerning him.

After the revelation of His saying: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell; you are to enter it.﴾ [al-Anbiya': 98] it became clear that the one who goes astray by worshipping other than Allah, he and his object of worship, will be in Hell together. ﴿Fuel of Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya': 98] means its firewood.

When this question reached our master Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, he said: "(ما) [mā] here refers to non-rational beings, so Jesus, 'Uzayr and the angels are not included in this ruling." This is the wisdom of Imam Ali, who was raised in the lap of the Prophet and learned in his school from his youth, and whose knowledge came from the light of prophethood.

Therefore the noble hadith has come down with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): And he was among the jurists, those of conscious deduction, even in front of the senior Companions, to the extent that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who used to bring down the Qur'an according to his opinion, stopped at a matter that no one could resolve except Ali. A case was put to him of a woman who gave birth after six months, and 'Umar ordered the hadd punishment to be carried out on her, because the well-known period of pregnancy is nine months.

Ali said: "O Commander of the Faithful, there is nothing upon her, because Allah says: ﴿And its carrying and weaning is thirty months﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 15] and He says: ﴿And mothers suckle their children for two complete years﴾ [al-Baqarah: 233]. So the period of pregnancy can be six months."

Another time he entered upon our master 'Umar with a whip, wanting to strike Hudhayfah with it. 'Umar said to him: "Why do I see you angry, O Commander of the Faithful?" He said: "I asked Hudhayfah, 'How did you wake up?' He said: 'I woke up loving temptation, disliking the truth, praying without wudu', and I have in the earth what Allah does not have in the heavens.'" Ali said: "He spoke the truth, by Allah, O Commander of the Faithful."

'Umar said: "Do you say this, O Abu al-Hasan?" He said: "As for temptation, Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And know that your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾ [al-Anfal: 28]. As for the truth he dislikes, it is death. As for praying without wudu', he sends blessings upon the Prophet (ﷺ) without wudu'. And he has in the earth a wife and a child, while Allah has no wife and no child."

At that 'Umar said: "Evil is the station in a land where Abu al-Hasan is not present."

Among the subtle sayings reported from him, may Allah be pleased with him, is that he passed by a group who disagreed about which of Allah's creatures is the strongest and most powerful. They asked him: "What is the strongest of Allah's soldiers, O Abu al-Hasan?" It was as if he already knew this question and knew he would be asked about it. So he said, counting the number before the things counted, and pointing with his hand that they were ten: the firm mountains; iron, which cuts mountains; fire, which melts iron; water, which extinguishes fire; the clouds, which carry water; the wind, which carries the clouds; the son of Adam, who overcomes the wind by covering himself with clothing and going on to his need; intoxication, which overcomes the son of Adam; sleep, which overcomes intoxication; and worry, which overcomes sleep. So the strongest of Allah's soldiers is worry.

In some of our discussions with the brothers, they asked me to mention to them the sermon of Imam Ali which he delivered when Fatimah, daughter of Muhammad, died. Whenever I mentioned it to them, they said, "Repeat it again." I said: When Fatimah died, she was buried beside the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Companions.

After she was buried, they said to him: "O Ali, if we permitted every child of the Messenger to be buried beside him, the mosque would become too crowded with people." He said: "Put her down by day, and I will move her by night, so that no strife arises." And at night he moved her to al-Baqi'.

Among what Imam Ali said while burying Fatimah beside her father, he said: "Peace be upon you, O Messenger of Allah, from me and from your daughter who has descended into your neighbourhood and who has quickly joined you. O Messenger of Allah, my patience over your chosen one has become scant, and my forbearance for her has become weak, except that in consoling myself over your calamity there is a place of solace. Indeed, I laid you down in the niche of your grave, and your soul departed between my chest and my throat. My night is sleepless, and my sorrow is everlasting, until Allah chooses for me the abode in which you dwell. Your daughter will inform you of the state of your nation, so question her thoroughly and ask her about their condition. This is said while the time since you departed is not long, and your memory has not left us."

When he wanted to leave, he said: "And peace be upon you both, the peace of one who bids farewell, neither weary nor tired. If I depart, it is not out of boredom, and if I stay, it is not out of ill thought about what Allah has promised to His patient servants."

The meaning of ﴿يَصِدُّونَ﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 57] (yaṣiddūn), i.e., they raise their voices with laughter and mockery of the Messenger of Allah.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 43, verse 58:

Meaning: their purpose in speaking about Jesus, 'Uzayr and the angels, and in asking whether our gods will enter the Fire along with them, was mere disputation (jadal). This is blameworthy disputation, because they wanted to justify their falsehood. So, disputation that is false is forbidden, whereas the praiseworthy disputation (jadal) that the Lawgiver prescribed is the constructive kind that leads to the truth.

Therefore the Truth said of them: ﴿Nay, they are a contentious people.﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 58] The meaning of (khasim) here: exaggeration in contention (khusumah), which is disputing by means of falsehood, obstinacy and stubbornness. We say: "So-and-so contended with me, and I defeated him (khasamtuhu)," meaning: I prevailed over him.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 43, verse 59:

﴿Inhu﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 59] here conveys negation, meaning: he (i.e., our master Jesus) is not ﴿except a servant﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 59], a servant of Allah like the rest of creation, meaning he is not a god as they claim. ﴿We bestowed Our favour upon him and made him a sign (mathal) for the Children of Israel﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 59]. Mathal means a lesson or a wonder among the wonders of creation that remains forever through the ages. Is it not wondrous that Jesus spoke in the cradle?

When his mother was questioned about him, she did not wish to speak, because her speech would not clear her of the people's accusation, so she pointed to him. Then they marvelled, ﴿How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a child?﴾ [Maryam: 29], so Jesus spoke while in his cradle: ﴿He said: Indeed, I am the servant of Allah﴾ [Maryam: 30].

So the first of his speech was to affirm his servanthood to Allah, and this is a matter that some Christians conceal, because it conflicts with their beliefs about the Messiah.

And it is remarkable that he then said, ﴿He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet﴾ [Maryam: 30], in the past tense, while he was still in his cradle. How? Allah had given him the Scripture and made him a prophet after he grew up, reached the age of responsibility, and bore the message. Thus what Allah wills will happen without fail, and Allah informed him of that while he was in his cradle.

The word ﴿servant﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 59] is the place of Allah's full bounty, so long as you devote your servanthood to Allah. This sincerity raised the righteous servant to the point that Moses, peace be upon him, walked in his train and learned from him, and Allah said of him: ﴿So they found one of Our servants, to whom We had given mercy from Us and taught him knowledge from Our presence﴾ [al-Kahf: 65].

In al-Isra' Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra': 1]. So servanthood is the place of giving, the giving of the message and what is above the message.

Here too, the servanthood of the Messiah was the place of ﴿We bestowed Our favour upon him﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 59]. With what? We bestowed Our favour upon him by choosing him for the message, and We created him in a manner without any previous precedent in creation. Therefore He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 50], meaning a wondrous miracle indicating the absoluteness of power.

And here He said ﴿and We made him a sign for the Children of Israel﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 59], because they are a materialistic people who do not believe in the unseen, and they always seek a material thing that falls under their senses.

Did they not say to Moses: ﴿Show us Allah openly﴾ [al-Nisa': 153], while He, glory be to Him, is unseen: ﴿No vision perceives Him, but He perceives all vision﴾ [al-An'am: 103].

When Allah sent down upon them the manna and the quail, which is among the finest and best foods, they said: ﴿O Moses, we will not endure one kind of food, so call upon your Lord to bring forth for us from what the earth grows: its herbs, its cucumbers, its garlic, its lentils, and its onions.﴾ He said: ﴿Would you exchange that which is lower for that which is better?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61].

Meaning: If the Truth, glorified is He, had willed, He would have made in place of them, that is, the Children of Israel, angels to succeed them in populating the earth. That would not happen except by their destruction and annihilation. This matter is not difficult for the power of God. In the verse there is evidence of the absoluteness of His power, and that He, glorified is He, does what He wills; so if He willed, He would act.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 43, verse 61:

﴿And indeed he﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 61], i.e., Jesus (peace be upon him), ﴿is a sign (ʿilm) of the Hour﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 61], meaning: an indication of its signs, which points to the nearness of its occurrence. ﴿So do not doubt it﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 61], do not be skeptical of it, nor dispute about its occurrence, for it is the truth about which there is no doubt.

﴿And follow me﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 61], be followers of me, convinced by my words and emulating me, for I am an exemplar for you in the course of life and in worship. ﴿This﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 61], i.e., what I have brought you, ﴿is a straight path﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 61].

The Almighty, glory be to Him, has made for the Hour clear signs that indicate it, because it is among the unseen matters that no one knows except Allah, and no one knows it. Everything we know about the Hour is its signs that indicate it.

What we believe about our master Jesus is that he is alive in heaven, and that he will descend to the earth.

In the hadith of the Night Journey (isra'), he descended and prayed behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). And he, although he is alive in heaven, will descend to the earth, die, and be buried.

We say to whoever opposes this matter, and says how Jesus is alive in heaven: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taken on the Night Journey and ascended to the heavens, and he remained there for a period of time, whether long or short. So when we say that Jesus is in heaven, the disagreement is only about the duration; and one who stays in heaven for an hour or two stays longer.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 43, verse 62:

That is: it should not prevent you or turn you away from the truth and guidance. ﴿Indeed, he is a clear enemy to you.﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 62] That is: his enmity is evident, and his enmity toward you is firmly established and ancient, dating back to your father Adam. So do not give him the opportunity to bar you from the truth or to open for you the doors of doubt, for he hunts for points of disagreement and hovers around them until he brings you into misguidance.

Indeed, it is he who said: ﴿I will surely sit in ambush for them on Your straight path﴾ [al-A'raf: 16]. That is: in the places of obedience, to corrupt them for them. And the Exalted One teaches us how to protect ourselves from him: ﴿And if an evil suggestion from Satan should come to you, then seek refuge in Allah﴾ [al-A'raf: 200]. So the name of Allah is what drives away from you the whispers of Satan and his prods, for the thought that comes from Satan has no lasting existence whatsoever in the presence of the thought that comes from the Most Merciful.

We have said: if a thief were hovering around your house and heard you say "Ihm" (a call to stop, "hush"), he would turn back and leave, even if you said it by mere coincidence. So whenever you feel that Satan is hovering around you, there is nothing for you to do but remember Allah and seek refuge in Him from his whispers.

You say: "A'udhu billahi min al-shaytan al-rajim" (I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan), saying it aloud. Satan himself has acknowledged that he has no authority over those who believe and devote themselves sincerely to Allah the Exalted: ﴿He said, "By Your might, I will surely mislead them all, * except Your sincere servants among them."﴾ [Sad: 82-83].

﴿بِٱلْبَيِّنَاتِ﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 63] the clear signs and miracles. ﴿قَالَ قَدْ جِئْتُكُم بِٱلْحِكْمَةِ﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 63] "He said: Indeed I have come to you with wisdom (al-hikma)," meaning: the Injil (Gospel) and the rulings it contains. ﴿وَلأُبَيِّنَ لَكُم بَعْضَ ٱلَّذِي تَخْتَلِفُونَ فِيهِ﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 63] "and to make clear to you some of that about which you differ." What they differed about was either before Jesus or after Jesus departed, for they said about him that he was the son of God, and they said: "the third of three." The Jews said even more than this.

God, glory be to Him, says: I gave him wisdom, meaning the Injil. Hikma means putting a thing in its proper place. Jesus, peace be upon him, came after Judaism, and Judaism had become excessively materialistic, and from it they proceeded in everything.

We have said that this materialism is what led them to ask their prophet to show them God: ﴿فَقَالُوۤاْ أَرِنَا ٱللَّهَ جَهْرَةً﴾ [An-Nisa: 153] "They said: Show us God openly." So there was no room for the unseen in their lives, even in their food and drink. When God sent down to them the manna and the quails (al-manna wa al-salwa), they were not content with it, and they wanted food that they could prepare with their own hands, so He said to them: ﴿ٱهْبِطُواْ مِصْراً فَإِنَّ لَكُمْ مَّا سَأَلْتُمْ﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 61] "Go down to a city, for indeed you will have what you asked for."

Therefore, when you read the Tawrah (Torah), you do not find in it any mention of the Last Day, and likewise the Talmud, although the Last Day and belief in it is a pillar of faith. But because of their materialism they do not believe in it. Therefore, when the message of Jesus, peace be upon him, came, it was entirely spiritual, to repair the spiritual deficiency in Judaism and so that the scale of balance in creation would be equal.

Therefore we do not find in the Injil anything about the regulations of society. If they wanted anything of that kind, they took it from the Tawrah. And they were compelled, despite the enmity between them, to combine the Tawrah and the Injil into one book, and they named it the Old Testament (al-'Ahd al-Qadim), because Jesus, peace be upon him, was once asked about inheritance and said: "I was not sent as a divider of inheritance."

So then: when materialism prevailed, he confronted it with spirituality, so that balance might occur in the movement of life, because spirituality is what drives material movement. Therefore the message of Jesus came to cultivate religious feelings and to raise people up through spiritual things.

Life needs both sides together: the material movement which interacts with the universe and nature. In the universe there are things that give you without your interacting with them, such as the sun, the moon, the stars, water and air; you are only a receiver. And there are other things that do not give you anything except when you interact with them, such as the earth, which you plant, plough and tend, and then it gives you crops.

And because Judaism went to extremes in materialism, Christianity likewise went to extremes in spirituality. Among the sayings of the Messiah, peace be upon him, is that when he saw them stoning a woman he said: "Whoever among you is without sin, let him cast the first stone," and he said: "Whoever strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him your left cheek."

This monasticism (rahbaniyya) was not prescribed for them by God; rather they took it upon themselves voluntarily, and the flaw in that is that they did not observe it as it should be observed. God, exalted is He, says: ﴿ثُمَّ قَفَّيْنَا عَلَىٰ آثَارِهِم بِرُسُلِنَا وَقَفَّيْنَا بِعِيسَى ٱبْنِ مَرْيَمَ وَآتَيْنَاهُ ٱلإِنجِيلَ وَجَعَلْنَا فِي قُلُوبِ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱتَّبَعُوهُ رَأْفَةً وَرَحْمَةً وَرَهْبَانِيَّةً ٱبتَدَعُوهَا مَا كَتَبْنَاهَا عَلَيْهِمْ إِلاَّ ٱبْتِغَآءَ رِضْوَانِ ٱللَّهِ فَمَا رَعَوْهَا حَقَّ رِعَايَتِهَا فَآتَيْنَا ٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُواْ مِنْهُمْ أَجْرَهُمْ وَكَثِيرٌ مِّنْهُمْ فَاسِقُونَ﴾ [Al-Hadid: 27] "Then We sent, following in their footsteps, Our messengers, and We sent after them Jesus, son of Mary, and gave him the Injil, and We placed in the hearts of those who followed him compassion and mercy, and monasticism which they invented; We did not prescribe it for them, except that they sought the pleasure of God. But they did not observe it with its proper observance. So We gave those of them who believed their reward, but many of them are defiantly disobedient."

So then: what was taken from them is not the monasticism itself; rather what was taken from them is that they did not observe it with its proper observance. And since Judaism went to extremes in materialism, and Christianity came as pure spirituality with nothing in it of regulations for organising society, it was necessary to correct both conditions, and the movement of life needed a new religion and a new message that takes account of both the spiritual and the material sides. That was the message of Islam.

Consider how the Qur'an gave an example of Muhammad and his community, once in the Tawrah and once in the Injil: ﴿مُّحَمَّدٌ رَّسُولُ ٱللَّهِ وَٱلَّذِينَ مَعَهُ أَشِدَّآءُ عَلَى ٱلْكُفَّارِ رُحَمَآءُ بَيْنَهُمْ تَرَاهُمْ رُكَّعاً سُجَّداً يَبْتَغُونَ فَضْلاً مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ وَرِضْوَاناً سِيمَاهُمْ فِي وُجُوهِهِمْ مِّنْ أَثَرِ ٱلسُّجُودِ ذَلِكَ مَثَلُهُمْ فِي ٱلتَّوْرَاةِ وَمَثَلُهُمْ فِي ٱلإِنجِيلِ كَزَرْعٍ أَخْرَجَ شَطْأَهُ فَآزَرَهُ فَٱسْتَغْلَظَ فَٱسْتَوَىٰ عَلَىٰ سُوقِهِ يُعْجِبُ ٱلزُّرَّاعَ لِيَغِيظَ بِهِمُ ٱلْكُفَّارَ﴾ [Al-Fath: 29] "Muhammad is the Messenger of God, and those with him are severe against the disbelievers and merciful among themselves. You see them bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from God and His pleasure. Their mark is on their faces from the traces of prostration. That is their likeness in the Tawrah, and their likeness in the Injil is like a seed that sends out its shoot, then strengthens it, so it grows thick and stands firm on its stem, pleasing the sowers, that He may enrage the disbelievers by them."

Thus the community of Islam combined spirit and matter. The Muslim is not shaped by harshness alone, nor by mercy alone; rather the situation shapes him. But severe against whom? And merciful towards whom?

Consider the precision of the Qur'anic expression in giving an example of the community of Islam in the Tawrah and in the Injil. Because the Jews were a materialistic people, He gave them the spiritual side in Islam: ﴿تَرَاهُمْ رُكَّعاً سُجَّداً يَبْتَغُونَ فَضْلاً مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ وَرِضْوَاناً سِيمَاهُمْ فِي وُجُوهِهِمْ مِّنْ أَثَرِ ٱلسُّجُودِ﴾ [Al-Fath: 29] "You see them bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from God and His pleasure. Their mark is on their faces from the traces of prostration."

As for the Injil, it mentioned the material side of Islam: ﴿كَزَرْعٍ أَخْرَجَ شَطْأَهُ فَآزَرَهُ فَٱسْتَغْلَظَ فَٱسْتَوَىٰ عَلَىٰ سُوقِهِ يُعْجِبُ ٱلزُّرَّاعَ لِيَغِيظَ بِهِمُ ٱلْكُفَّارَ﴾ [Al-Fath: 29] "like a seed that sends out its shoot, then strengthens it, so it grows thick and stands firm on its stem, pleasing the sowers, that He may enrage the disbelievers by them."

So it is as if Islam, by combining materialism and spirituality, is the appropriate and sound method for leading the movement of life. Spirituality is never upright without materiality. The worshipper, for example, does not sustain his worship except with a loaf of bread that sustains his life and a garment that covers his nakedness. From where does he get the loaf? From where does he get the garment? The loaf needs a farmer who plants and harvests, and needs a mill, and a bakery and workers, and so on; and likewise the garment, all of which is material movement.

Therefore God, glory be to Him, made the Qur'an a guardian (muhayminan) over the previous books: ﴿وَمُهَيْمِناً عَلَيْهِ﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 48] "and a guardian over it." And He said: ﴿وَإِنَّهُ فِيۤ أُمِّ ٱلْكِتَابِ لَدَيْنَا لَعَلِيٌّ حَكِيمٌ﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 4] "And indeed it is, in the Mother of the Book with Us, exalted and full of wisdom," meaning: it rises above all the heavenly books.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وَلأُبَيِّنَ لَكُم بَعْضَ ٱلَّذِي تَخْتَلِفُونَ فِيهِ﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 63] "and to make clear to you some of that about which you differ" refers to things that were forbidden to the Jews, which God made lawful for them, such as camels, as He said: ﴿وَلأُحِلَّ لَكُم بَعْضَ ٱلَّذِي حُرِّمَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 50] "and to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you." And He said: ﴿وَعَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ هَادُواْ حَرَّمْنَا كُلَّ ذِي ظُفُرٍ وَمِنَ ٱلْبَقَرِ وَٱلْغَنَمِ حَرَّمْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ شُحُومَهُمَآ إِلاَّ مَا حَمَلَتْ ظُهُورُهُمَا أَوِ ٱلْحَوَايَآ أَوْ مَا ٱخْتَلَطَ بِعَظْمٍ﴾ [Al-An'am: 146] "And to those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws, and of cattle and sheep We forbade them their fats, except what their backs carried, or the entrails, or what is mixed with bone."

Here we note the use of the detached pronoun ﴿He﴾, which indicates restriction (qasr). Allah is my Lord, and none other is a lord for me or for you. ﴿So worship Him﴾ because He is the truth. ﴿This﴾, that is, what I call you to, ﴿is a straight path﴾, a sound road with no crookedness in it.

We have said that the straight path is the balanced (ʿidl) road that brings you to the goal by the shortest distance and with the least hardship. If the road brings you from a starting point to a destination, then the road to Allah brings you from Allah to Allah: from Allah as a obligation (taklif), and to Allah as fruit and reward, where the return is to Him alone.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 43, verse 65:

﴿Al-aḥzāb﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 65] is the plural of ḥizb (a party, faction), meaning a group of people united by one thought and one belief. The divergence of the factions shows that they are in error, and that they are the factions of Satan, because the party of God is one: it takes its thought and its beliefs from the Book of God: ﴿Those are the party of God. Surely the party of God are the successful ones﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 22].

﴿So woe to those who have done wrong, from the punishment of a painful day﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 65]. Wayl (woe) means destruction. Destruction from whom? From God. And the act, as we have said, is measured by the power of the agent, so what then if the punishment and the destruction come from God?

It is also said that wayl is a valley in Hell. ﴿For those who have done wrong﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 65], meaning they wronged themselves through appetites and sins, or they wronged others among people. ﴿From the punishment of a painful day﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 65]. So consider the punishment itself, when the day on which the punishment occurs is a painful day: how then will the punishment be?

The punishment is described as ʼalīm (painful), meaning painful to the sense. It is described as muqīm (lasting), meaning permanent, never ceasing. It is described as ʻaẓīm (great) and shadīd (severe), and it is described as muhīn (humiliating) for whoever God wishes to humiliate and abase beyond the punishment. Thus: for every sinner is the punishment that suits him.

Al-Sha'rawi, Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66), on surah 43, verse 66:

That is: they await nothing but the Hour, i.e., the Resurrection, ﴿that it come upon them suddenly﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 66], i.e., unexpectedly, ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 66]. So when it is known that it will come suddenly, preparation for it becomes obligatory, since no one knows its appointed time. ﴿None can reveal its time except Him﴾ [al-A'raf: 187].

And we have said: the vagueness of the Resurrection and the vagueness of death is itself clarity and the utmost explanation. The vagueness of time enlarges the admonition, so that you prepare and await it at every moment; likewise the vagueness of cause and the vagueness of place. ﴿And no soul knows in what land it will die﴾ [Luqman: 34]. Death without apparent causes is itself the cause.

The discussion here is about the Day of Resurrection, when the standards of brotherhood and close friendship are reversed. As for His saying, ﴿The close friends﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 67], it is the plural of *khalil* (close, intimate friend), meaning the companion whom you love and cherish so deeply that it is as if you have entered into his limbs and mingled with his flesh and blood, as the poet said:

*When we met, longing brought its utmost effort,*
*Two intimate friends melting with anguish and reproach.*

*As if one intimate friend had slipped into the inner being of the other,*
*Vanished within the embrace and was lost.*

*Khullah* (deep friendship) may be in goodness or in evil. The friendship of goodness is that which helps you to follow God's way. The true *khalil* is the one who, if he sees you doing good, helps you, and if he sees you otherwise, advises you and takes you by the hand.

God says, describing those who believe: ﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds, and enjoin one another to truth, and enjoin one another to patience﴾ [al-'Asr: 3].

These are the friends whom the Messenger of God meant in the noble hadith. This is the friendship of truth and the friendship of sincerity, whose love endures in this world and continues until the Day of Resurrection. They are friends in this world and friends in the Hereafter.

As for the friends in evil, who unite over desires and over violating the sanctities of God, their friendship turns in the Hereafter into enmity and hatred, as each of them blames his companion. The evil they came together upon in this world destroyed them in the Hereafter, and the sins for whose sake they loved one another are what cast them into the lasting punishment.

So each of them sees the other as an enemy, because he did not restrain him or forbid him. From here Islam gave great attention to choosing a friend and a companion, and taught us how to choose a righteous companion and a righteous associate.

Thus, on the Day of Recompense, the falsehood of relationships is revealed, and only the bonds of goodness that connect one brother to another remain. The noble Qur'an, in more than one place, depicts for us what passes between those who were friends in this world and enemies in the Hereafter.

Among that is His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve will say: "Our Lord, show us those who misled us from the jinn and mankind, that we may place them beneath our feet so that they will be among the lowest."﴾ [Fussilat: 29].

The word ʿabd (عبد) has the plurals ʿabīd (عبيد) and ʿibād (عباد), and each has its own meaning. ʿAbīd includes all people, believer and disbeliever, obedient and disobedient, because they are all ʿabīd in the sense of being subjected to God in matters of compulsion from which no one can ever escape, such as sickness, death and other things. We all share in these, and we are all ʿabīd in this sense.

As for ʿibād, they are the elite who chose God, devoted their worship sincerely to Him, and gave up their own choice for the choice of their Lord and His will, and so they earned this rank.

﴿O My servants (yā ʿibādi)﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 68]. God attributed them to Himself and joined them to His own Essence, exalted is He. The word ʿibād does not occur with any meaning other than this except in one place, in the context of speaking about the Day of Resurrection: ﴿Did you lead these, My servants (ʿibādī), astray?﴾ [Al-Furqan: 17]. Here He called them ʿibād even though they were astray. They said: this is because the discussion here concerns the Day of Resurrection, when no one has any choice left as to whether to believe or disbelieve; everyone there is obedient without any choice, so He called them ʿibād.

So the Truth, glory be to Him, honours us with this address, ﴿O My servants (yā ʿibādi)﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 68], and ennobles us by being ascribed to Him, glory be to Him, in the manner of the poet's saying:

"Among what has increased me in honour and might, and I nearly walked upon the Pleiades with my soles:
My entering under your saying, 'O My servants,' and that you made Aḥmad a prophet for me."

As for His saying: ﴿No fear shall be upon you this Day, nor shall you grieve﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 68]. Yes, what fear is there when we are servants of God? What fear could befall us after we have clung to Him, exalted is He? Do we not say in this world: "No distress, and You are the Lord"? So: ﴿No fear shall be upon you this Day, nor shall you grieve﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 68], i.e., over what you have missed of the bounties of this world, because you are turning toward what is better and more lasting than the bounties of this world.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 43, verse 69:

This verse shows that there is a difference between iman (faith) and islam (submission). Iman is the work of the heart, while islam is the work of the limbs that carry out the method (manhaj) that Allah has commanded you to follow. For this reason we see that the hypocrites (munafiqun) were the first of people to come to prayer, even though their hearts were not like that.

Consider His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed." Say, "You have not believed; but say, 'We have submitted,'"﴾ [al-Hujurat: 14]. For this reason they used to stand in the first row, to clear themselves of the accusation of hypocrisy. It is remarkable that hypocrisy appeared in Madinah, the land of the Ansar and the starting point of Islam, and did not appear in Makkah, the stronghold of disbelief and idols, and the country most hostile to Islam.

When we reflected on this phenomenon, we said: hypocrisy only appears in the presence of a power that inspires awe, so whoever is hypocritical towards it shows himself. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) became in Madinah a power that inspires awe, with might, supporters and an army. In Makkah, however, he was in a position of weakness and persecution, so why would anyone be hypocritical towards him?

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿those who believed in Our signs﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 69], meaning: their hearts were convinced by them. Conviction has degrees: knowledge of certainty (ilm al-yaqin), when someone you trust in his truthfulness informs you; eye of certainty (ayn al-yaqin), when you witness a thing with your own eyes; and truth of certainty (haqq al-yaqin), when you directly experience it and test it with your own senses.

I recall that I once travelled to Indonesia and saw there banana fingers, each finger half a metre long. I was amazed, and on my return to Egypt I took some with me so that my children could see them. When I returned, I said to them, "Imagine, in Indonesia I saw such and such." Of course they were amazed, since they knew that I do not lie to them. This is called knowledge of certainty.

Then I said to them: "Open this suitcase." They opened it and found within it banana fingers just as I had told them. This is called eye of certainty. When they took them out, tasted their flavour and handled their texture and colour, the matter became truth of certainty, and so on.

So whoever believes with knowledge of certainty, does he carry out what he believes? The one who acts and carries it out is a Muslim, and the one who does not carry it out is a hypocrite, because he believed with his tongue and did not act upon what he believed.

When the Bedouins heard this verse, they were reassured that they would believe in the future, because they knew the meaning of (lamma) ("not yet"), which expresses the negation of the past and present but not the future.

So His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed." Say, "You have not believed; but say, 'We have submitted,' for faith has not yet entered your hearts"﴾ [al-Hujurat: 14], means: it will enter later.

This is the reward: the reward of those who believed and were Muslims. On the Day of Resurrection, Allah will say to them: ﴿Enter the Garden, you and your spouses, delighted﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 70]. He specified the spouses because every pleasure a person enjoys and is gladdened by stirs in him the instincts of youthful desire, and he inclines to have a wife who shares his enjoyment and joy, and so it is.

Thus the spouse, whether husband or wife, is first the companion who is desired, and second the helper in tranquility (sakan), affection (mawaddah) and mercy (rahmah). Tranquility and affection are well known between the spouses, but mercy, when is it?

Mercy we see between the spouses in the period of old age and senility, when each of them is in need of mercy from the other. Mercy comes before any other feelings.

As for the meaning of ﴿tuhbarun﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 70]: al-hubur (intense joy) is a kind of clarity, radiance and brightness that rises on a person's face when he rejoices with a joy that nothing troubles, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾ [Al-Mutaffifin: 24].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 43, verse 71:

The discussion here is about the bliss of Paradise. Al-sihaf (ṣiḥāf) is the plural of ṣaḥfah, which is the wide dish (ṭabaq) from which the whole family eats. Larger than it is the qaṣʿah, and larger than the qaṣʿah is the jafnah. Accordingly, the noble Hadith reports that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spoke of Ibn Jud'an, that he had a jafnah so large that one could take shade in its shadow from the heat of the sun.

In the story of Sulayman (peace be upon him) and the jinn whom Allah subjected to his service, Allah the Exalted says: ﴿They made for him whatever he willed: sanctuaries, statues, basins like reservoirs, and fixed cooking pots...﴾ [Saba': 13].

Likewise, in Paradise there are sihaf, but made of gold.

﴿And cups﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 71]: the plural of kūb, which is a vessel from which one drinks that has no handle. There are also al-abariq, the plural of ibriq, which is a vessel from which one drinks that has a handle and a spout at its top. And there is the ka's, which is the kūb when it is full of drink.

﴿And therein is whatever the souls desire, and delightful to the eyes﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 71]. This is a concise description of a multitude whose details would take a long time to mention. What is served on these sihaf and in these akwab of food and drink that the souls desire—this is in terms of taste.

﴿And delightful to the eyes﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 71]: meaning, its colour is pleasing and beautiful to your eye; merely looking at it is a delight, so what of its taste and flavour? Thus, when you host a dear guest, for example, you say to him: "What would you like to eat?" Why? So that you may prepare for him what his soul desires and inclines to.

That is to say, the matter is not merely (filling the belly). You will notice that He mentioned the sihaf first, then the akwab, because a person usually eats and then drinks, so there is an ordering of importance.

He also mentioned the delight of the eyes in food, because by looking at it you find a pleasure that may surpass the pleasure of eating. Therefore Allah says in another place: ﴿Look at its fruit when it bears fruit﴾ [al-An'am: 99], combining with the delight of eating the delight of looking at it.

And His words: ﴿And you therein will abide forever﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 71], because this is an abode of permanence and immortality, where there is no death and no cutting off of blessing, so the blessing does not escape you nor do you escape it. That is to say, a pure delight that nothing spoils, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Neither cut off nor forbidden﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 33], because it is the gift of Allah, and the gift of Allah is lasting and never ceases.

On His words ﴿You have inherited it﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 72]: you have taken it as an inheritance (irth). Inheritance occurs after the death of its owner, like a deceased person who dies and leaves his property and estate to those after him, such as his children and relatives. So these people possess the estate without a contract and without a price. But whom have they inherited from?

He, may He be exalted, says in another verse: ﴿Those are the inheritors, who will inherit Paradise (al-Firdaws); therein they will abide forever﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 10-11]. They said: when Allah, glorified and exalted, created creation, He counted them numerically and wrote everything in the eternal decree (al-miqat al-azali), and it is established that the pen has dried over that.

When al-Ma'mun was asked: what is your Lord occupied with now, since it is established that the pen has dried? He said: matters He brings forth and does not initiate; He raises some peoples and lowers others.

They said regarding this matter of inheritance that the believers in Paradise have inherited the disbelievers and taken their places in Paradise, because Allah, glorified and exalted, has assigned to every human being a place in Paradise and a place in Hell. Even if all of creation came as believers who obey, there would be places in Paradise sufficient for them, and likewise if they all disbelieved, places would exist for them in the Fire.

So at the moment the people of the Fire enter the Fire, their places in Paradise become vacant, and Allah, glorified and exalted, makes them the right of the believers and bestows them upon them as inheritance, first by His grace and generosity, then as a reward for their excellence in faith and righteous deeds in this world.

Therefore He said: ﴿You have inherited it because of what you used to do﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 72]. So righteous deeds are thus the fundamental basis for entering Paradise and for inheriting the places of the people of the Fire.

We observe in the matter of inheritance that it transfers the ownership of a thing from the one who bequeaths it to his heir, and this inheritance is lawful for the heir regardless of its source, whether from lawful or unlawful means. If a man earned wealth unlawfully, he bears its burden alone and will be encircled with it on the Day of Resurrection.

If it passes to the heir, it is lawful for him, and nothing is upon him in it, because the responsibility here does not extend. Our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), settled this matter when he said: the heir is not obliged to ask about the source of the wealth he inherited. He is like a wife who does not ask her husband about the source of the maintenance he gives her, and like a child below puberty who may not ask his father where the money he spends on him comes from.

But the child has that right once he reaches maturity and becomes able to earn, so he may ask, because he has become able to earn lawfully by himself.

This is by analogy with His words: ﴿And when the children among you reach puberty, let them ask permission as those before them asked permission﴾ [al-Nur: 59]. So after puberty, he no longer has a right over his father; rather the right has passed from him to his father, unless the father chooses to show grace.

We have said that the matter of the father's graciousness has negatively affected our economies, because the excessive tenderness of fathers and the pampering of children has caused the period of childhood to extend in our youth to the age of twenty-five, even thirty. The child in it is a burden on his father, wanting everything from him, even the apartment, the furniture, and the marriage. Our youth have inclined to comfort and cast responsibility upon their fathers, and this wastes on us many energies that are not utilized.

Therefore the West has surpassed us in this matter: at such an age the young person there goes out into life and the field of work, bears his responsibility himself, and becomes entirely independent of the family. True, they have erred in this matter by equating the boy and the girl, because the girl has a different situation. Therefore here we embrace her until she marries, so she leaves her father's house only for her husband's house.

سبق أن ذكر الحق سبحانه الطعام والشراب في الجنة، وأنها في صِحَاف وفي أكواب، وهذه معروفة للعرب. وهنا يذكر أن من نِعَم الجنة الفاكهة، والعرب لم تكن تعهد الفاكهة ولا تعرف الكثير منها، لذلك خَصَّ الفاكهة بعد ذكر الطعام والشراب. والفاكهة بعد الطعام والشراب دليل على الرفاهية والمتعة التامة، والفاكهة من التفكّه. يعني: ليست من الضروريات، بل من الرفاهية (فنطظية يعني).

الحق سبحانه وتعالى أعطانا ضروريات الحياة من المأكل والمشرب والملبس، ثم زادنا ما نُرفِّه به حياتنا. اقرأ مثلاً: ﴿يَا بَنِي آدَمَ قَدْ أَنزَلْنَا عَلَيْكُمْ لِبَاساً يُوَارِي سَوْءَاتِكُمْ وَرِيشاً وَلِبَاسُ التَّقْوَىٰ ذَٰلِكَ خَيْرٌ..﴾ [الأعراف: 26]. فاللباس الذي يُواري السوءة من الضروريات، والرياش للزينة والترفُّه. ثم نبَّه إلى ما هو أهمّ من اللباس المادي، إنه اللباس المعنوي الذي يسترك في دنياك وأُخراك، إنه لباس التقوى.

وبعد أن أعطانا الحق سبحانه صورة موجزة لأهل الجنة وبعض ما فيها من نعيم، ليعطينا المقابل لتتضح الصورة أكثر، وهذه سِمَة من سمات الأسلوب القرآني، لأن النفس حين تُذكر لها ما تنبسط له، ثم تُذكر ما تنقبض له، يظهر لها الفرق، مثل قوله تعالى: ﴿إِنَّ الْأَبْرَارَ لَفِي نَعِيمٍ * وَإِنَّ الْفُجَّارَ لَفِي جَحِيمٍ﴾ [الانفطار: 13-14].

وهنا يقول تعالى:

﴿إِنَّ الْمُجْرِمِينَ...﴾.

Almighty Allah establishes for us three realities about the criminals: that they abide eternally in the punishment, so it is a punishment that is extended with no end to it. Then ﴿They will not be relieved of it﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 75], meaning: it will not be lightened for them; ﴿and they will be in it despairing﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 75], meaning: they will be full of anguish and despondent about deliverance, despairing of good, with no hope in their hearts of ever leaving it. Thus He has gathered upon them every aspect of pain, anguish, despair and the severing of hope.
